case_name: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms. Mamta Binani
holding_summary: In the Rolta India Limited CIRP, the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner's appeal against the NCLT's plan-approval order was dismissed by NCLAT as time-barred because it was e-filed one day beyond the maximum 45-day period (30 days plus 15 condonable days) under Section 61(2) of the IBC. The appellant showed its first attempt to e-file, on 29 January 2026, failed because of a technical defect on the NCLAT's own portal backend, and the appeal only went through the next day. The Supreme Court held a litigant should not be shown the door because of the tribunal's own e-filing system failure, and restored the matter to NCLAT to decide afresh whether sufficient cause exists to condone the delay, treating the first bona fide attempt as the effective date of presentation.
why_it_matters: Gives litigants a concrete precedent to invoke when a tribunal's own e-filing portal causes a marginal delay in a limitation-sensitive IBC appeal, without needing to separately prove the glitch was anything more than a bona fide, documented first attempt.

case_name: Fortune Resources and Properties LLP v. Y.P. Goel and Associates and Anr.
citation: MA No. 105 of 2025, Chhattisgarh High Court, decided 21 August 2026
holding_summary: A complainant alleged an oral agreement to buy a shop in a Raipur commercial project for Rs. 75 lakh, with part payment later refunded after possession and a sale deed never materialised. RERA dismissed the complaint for want of a written allotment agreement and held it lacked jurisdiction; REAT reversed, holding the complainant was still an 'aggrieved person' and remanding for fresh consideration. The Chhattisgarh High Court, dismissing the builder's appeal under Section 58 of RERA, held that the term 'aggrieved person' under Section 31 of the Act and Rule 35 of the Rules is of wide amplitude, and the mere absence of a written allotment document or agreement does not by itself oust RERA's jurisdiction over a real estate complaint.
why_it_matters: Prevents developers from defeating a RERA complaint on a pure documentation technicality, and signals that buyers who paid on the strength of an oral or informal booking can still invoke RERA rather than being pushed into ordinary civil litigation.

case_name: Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd. v. Haryana Power Purchase Centre / Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission
holding_summary: HERC had directed HPPC to pay a higher tariff of Rs. 6.44/kWh to Siwana Solar Power Projects Ltd. for its 5 MW solar project in Bhiwani, Haryana, operating under a February 2014 power purchase agreement. APTEL, per Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat, set aside HERC's order and held that Rs. 5.68/kWh was the binding tariff applicable to the project under the governing PPA and tariff regulations.
why_it_matters: A reminder to solar developers and procurers that APTEL will hold parties to the tariff fixed under the originally governing PPA/regulations rather than a later, more favourable state commission redetermination, with real cash-flow consequences on a per-unit basis across a project's life.

case_name: N. Balakrishnan v. Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Ors.
holding_summary: The petitioner sought to quash a TNRERA order granting project registration over a Thiruneermalai, Tambaram property that he claimed to own. Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy held that TNRERA cannot adjudicate disputed questions of title while examining a project registration application, and that a party disputing ownership must approach the competent civil court; TNRERA may refuse registration only where the absence of title or an encumbrance is apparent on the face of the record.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that RERA project registration is not a judicial finding of clear title, so a person disputing a developer's ownership cannot rely on RERA proceedings to resolve the title question and must pursue a separate civil suit.

case_name: Hari Prakash v. New Delhi Municipal Council
holding_summary: NDMC challenged a Labour Court award holding that its Driver-cum-Field Worker's services were illegally terminated, awarding Rs. 75,000 compensation. The Delhi High Court dismissed the challenge, reiterating that an employer cannot establish that a workman has abandoned service merely by alleging he stopped reporting for duty; voluntary abandonment requires proof of actual intention to abandon, established through adequate evidence and surrounding circumstances placed before the Labour Court.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that employers bear the burden of affirmatively proving intention to abandon employment with evidence, not bare assertion, before they can treat an absent workman as having abandoned service rather than being illegally terminated.

case_name: ASR Market Ventures Private Limited v. Fitship Private Limited & Anr.
citation: C.O. (COMM.IPD-TM) 93/2025, Delhi High Court, decided 31 August 2026
holding_summary: ASR Market Ventures (owner of FITPASS) sought rectification of Fitship's registered 'FITFEAST' mark and an interim injunction in a connected passing-off suit, claiming it had coined FITFEAST in 2017. Justice Jyoti Singh dismissed the rectification petition and refused the interim injunction, holding ASR's own records showed it had consistently promoted its business under the umbrella mark FITPASS, with only scant, non-source-identifying references to FITFEAST, so ASR failed to establish goodwill in FITFEAST as a standalone mark.
why_it_matters: Shows that merely coining or occasionally using a term alongside a dominant house mark is not enough to claim standalone trademark rights in it — a business must show the secondary mark was itself used to identify source before it can rely on that mark against a later, independently adopted registration.

case_name: M. Gagan Bothra v. Senthil Kumar
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai Bench
holding_summary: A financial creditor, M. Gagan Bothra, filed a Section 95 IBC application against Senthil Kumar as personal guarantor of the corporate debtor, PRC International Hotels Private Limited. Senthil Kumar resisted the petition partly on the ground that he resided abroad. The NCLT, Chennai Bench (Judicial Member Sanjiv Jain and Technical Member Venkataraman Subramaniam), admitted the Section 95 petition, holding that the IBC does not restrict its applicability to personal guarantors based on nationality or place of residence, particularly where the guarantee was executed with a Chennai address and the underlying corporate debtor was based in Chennai.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that an NRI or overseas-resident personal guarantor cannot resist a Section 95 IBC petition merely by pointing to foreign residence or citizenship, giving financial creditors a clearer basis to pursue personal guarantors who have relocated abroad.
